problem: Step 8 says 'Check QᵀQ = I gives QᵀAQ = diag(1, 3)'. Orthogonality of Q does not imply QᵀAQ = D. QᵀQ = I only proves the columns are orthonormal; QᵀAQ = D holds only because those columns are eigenvectors placed in the same order as the eigenvalues in D. A student will read this as an implication and repeat the mistake.
fix: Split the two checks. Step 8: QᵀQ = I, so Q is orthogonal. Step 9: compute AQ and QD (or QᵀAQ directly) and show they are equal, giving QᵀAQ = diag(1, 3). State that QᵀAQ = D follows from the columns being eigenvectors matched to the diagonal entries, not from QᵀQ = I alone.

problem: 'A general matrix may lack eigenvectors' is imprecise. Over the complex numbers every square matrix has at least one eigenvector; what a general real matrix may lack is a full set of real eigenvectors (a rotation matrix has none), and it may need complex eigenvalues.
fix: Write: 'A general real matrix may have complex eigenvalues, and may have too few real eigenvectors to form a basis.'
